segments.text: Euclid's Elements, Book One, Proposition Thirty-Two. In any triangle, an exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles, and the three interior angles sum to two right angles. Let A B C be a triangle, and let side B C be extended to D. We prove that the exterior angle A C D equals the sum of the opposite interior angles C A B and A B C, and that the three interior angles A B C, B C A, and C A B sum to two right angles.

segments.text: Since segment A B is parallel to segment C E and transversal A C falls upon them, by Proposition Twenty-Nine, the alternate interior angles C A B and A C E are equal. Again, since segment A B is parallel to segment C E and line B D falls upon them, the exterior angle E C D equals the opposite interior angle A B C. Adding these equals, the whole exterior angle A C D equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles C A B and A B C. Now add the interior angle B C A to each. Then the sum of angles A C D and B C A equals the sum of the three interior angles A B C, B C A, and C A B. Yet by Proposition Thirteen, the adjacent angles A C D and B C A on line B D sum to two right angles. Therefore the three interior angles of triangle A B C equal two right angles, as was required to prove.
